Sodium: Physiology and dietary sources


Proximal tubule
60–70% of the ﬁltered sodium is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. The whole process is possible largely due to the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase.
The main transporter through which Naþ is reabsorbed from the luminal side is the Naþ/Hþ exchanger (NHE) (Alpern, 1985) in the
proximal convoluted tubule (PCT). In addition, the negatively charged interstitium serves as a driving force for the paracellular reab-
sorption of Naþ, which is facilitated by rather leaky tight junctions of the proximal tubule. As matter of fact, the passive reabsorption
of Naþ in the proximal tubule can even exceed the active one, accounting for up to 2/3 of the total (Alpern et al., 1985; Seldin et al.,
1991). Other mechanisms that contribute to Naþ-reabsorption in the proximal tubule are cotransporters of Naþ and other mole-
cules like glucose (mainly through the SGLT2) amino acids, phosphate, lactate and sulfate (Petrovic et al., 2004) (Fig. 2).
Factors that upregulate Naþ reabsorption are cytosolic acidosis, Angiotensin II and sympathetic innervation. Factors that down-
